A_target.statement:
Let $C$ be a [[Definition:Circle|circle]] with center $O$.
Let $\angle APB$ be an [[Definition:Inscribed Angle|inscribed angle]] subtending the arc $AB$.
Then:
:$\angle APB = \dfrac 1 2 \angle AOB$

B_source.statement:
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a [[Definition:Triangle (Geometry)|triangle]].
Then an [[Definition:Exterior Angle of Polygon|exterior angle]] of $\triangle ABC$ equals the sum of the two [[Definition:Opposite (in Triangle)|non-adjacent]] interior angles.

substitutions.the isosceles triangle: the triangle formed by two radii and a chord to the inscribed vertex

derived.base angle: the inscribed angle (for the simple case)

object_map.reformulation: Draw the radius to the inscribed vertex, splitting the configuration into isosceles triangles, then apply the exterior-angle relation.

validity_conditions: Radii to the arc endpoints and to the inscribed vertex form isosceles triangles (two sides are radii, hence equal).
The exterior-angle theorem gives each central sub-angle as twice the corresponding inscribed sub-angle.
Summing (or differencing) the sub-cases covers all positions of the inscribed vertex relative to the center.
proof_plan:
Join $O$ to $P$ and extend $PO$ to meet the circle at $Q$.
$OA = OP = OB$ are [[Definition:Radius of Circle|radii]], so $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$ are [[Definition:Isosceles Triangle|isosceles]].

In $\triangle OAP$ the base angles are equal: $\angle OAP = \angle OPA$.
By the source result, the exterior angle $\angle AOQ = \angle OAP + \angle OPA = 2 \angle OPA$.
Similarly $\angle BOQ = 2 \angle OPB$.
The base angles $\angle OPA$ and $\angle OPB$ are the parts of the inscribed angle $\angle APB$ on either side of $PQ$.
